claim: Wnt signaling plays important roles in development, homeostasis, and tumorigenesis.
source: Wnt signaling plays important roles in development, homeostasis, and tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a general statement about Wnt signaling that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Mutations in β-catenin that activate Wnt signaling have been found in colorectal and hepatocellular carcinomas.
source: Mutations in β-catenin that activate Wnt signaling have been found in colorectal and hepatocellular carcinomas.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about cancer mutations.

claim: The dynamics of wild-type and mutant forms of β-catenin are not fully understood.
source: However, the dynamics of wild-type and mutant forms of β-catenin are not fully understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Wild-type and oncogenic mutant alleles of β-catenin were tagged with different fluorescent proteins in a colorectal cancer cell line.
source: Here, we genome-engineered fluorescently tagged alleles of endogenous β-catenin in a colorectal cancer cell line. Wild-type and oncogenic mutant alleles were tagged with different fluorescent proteins, enabling the analysis of both variants in the same cell.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: Wild-type and mutant β-catenin alleles have distinctly different biophysical properties.
source: We analyzed the properties of both β-catenin alleles using immunoprecipitation, immunofluorescence, and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy approaches, revealing distinctly different biophysical properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data using multiple analytical techniques.

claim: Activation of Wnt signaling by treatment with a GSK3β inhibitor modulated the wild-type allele to mimic the properties of the mutant β-catenin allele.
source: In addition, activation of Wnt signaling by treatment with a GSK3β inhibitor or a truncating APC mutation modulated the wild-type allele to mimic the properties of the mutant β-catenin allele.
evidence: This describes experimental results from drug treatment studies.

claim: A truncating APC mutation modulated the wild-type allele to mimic the properties of the mutant β-catenin allele.
source: In addition, activation of Wnt signaling by treatment with a GSK3β inhibitor or a truncating APC mutation modulated the wild-type allele to mimic the properties of the mutant β-catenin allele.
evidence: This describes experimental results from genetic manipulation studies.

claim: Wnt signaling pathways play fundamental roles in many biological processes in development, stem cell maintenance, and disease.
source: Wnt signaling pathways play fundamental roles in many biological processes in development, stem cell maintenance, and disease (Clevers and Nusse, 2012; Zhan et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: β-catenin (CTNNB1) is a key regulator of canonical Wnt signaling.
source: A key regulator of "canonical" Wnt signaling is β-catenin (CTNNB1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Wnt signaling pathway.

claim: When Wnt signaling is inactive, β-catenin forms part of the destruction complex.
source: When Wnt signaling is inactive, β-catenin forms part of the destruction complex, which consists of adenomatous polyposis coli (APC), axis inhibition protein 1 (Axin1) (Li et al., 2012), casein kinase 1α (CK1α), and glycogen synthase kinase 3β (GSK3β).
evidence: This describes the composition of the destruction complex with citation support.

claim: The destruction complex consists of APC, Axin1, CK1α, and GSK3β.
source: When Wnt signaling is inactive, β-catenin forms part of the destruction complex, which consists of adenomatous polyposis coli (APC), axis inhibition protein 1 (Axin1) (Li et al., 2012), casein kinase 1α (CK1α), and glycogen synthase kinase 3β (GSK3β).
evidence: This lists the components of the destruction complex with citation support.

claim: In the destruction complex, β-catenin is N-terminally phosphorylated at Ser45 by CK1 kinase.
source: In the destruction complex, β-catenin is N-terminally phosphorylated at Ser45 by CK1 kinase (Hagen and Vidal-Puig, 2002) and then sequentially phosphorylated at residues Ser33, Ser37, and Thr41 by GSK3β (Liu et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes a specific phosphorylation event supported by citation.

claim: β-catenin is sequentially phosphorylated at residues Ser33, Ser37, and Thr41 by GSK3β.
source: In the destruction complex, β-catenin is N-terminally phosphorylated at Ser45 by CK1 kinase (Hagen and Vidal-Puig, 2002) and then sequentially phosphorylated at residues Ser33, Ser37, and Thr41 by GSK3β (Liu et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes sequential phosphorylation events supported by citation.

claim: Phospho-β-catenin is targeted to proteasomal degradation by the SCFßTrCP E3-ligase complex.
source: Subsequently, phospho-β-catenin is targeted to proteasomal degradation by the SCFßTrCP E3-ligase complex (Wu et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the degradation mechanism supported by citation.

claim: Wnt signaling is activated when Wnt ligands bind to Frizzled protein family receptors and the LRP5/6 co-receptor.
source: Wnt signaling is activated when Wnt ligands bind to seven-pass transmembrane receptors of the Frizzled (Fzd) protein family and the transmembrane LRP5/6 (low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein) co-receptor (Bilic et al., 2007; Cong et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of Wnt pathway activation supported by citations.

claim: Fzd proteins recruit the cytosolic adaptor protein Dishevelled (Dvl) to the cell membrane via its DEP domain, leading to polymerization of Dvl.
source: Fzd proteins then recruit the cytosolic adaptor protein Dishevelled (Dvl) to the cell membrane via its DEP domain, leading to polymerization of Dvl (Schwarz-Romond et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes a molecular mechanism supported by citation.

claim: Dvl facilitates membrane recruitment of Axin1 by a DIX-DIX domain heterotypic interaction.
source: Dvl facilitates membrane recruitment of Axin1 by a DIX-DIX domain heterotypic interaction (Cliffe et al., 2003), which in turn stimulates GSK3β- and CK1α-mediated phosphorylation of the LRP5/6 cytosolic tail in its five PPPSPxS motifs and its binding to LRP5/6 (Stamos et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes a protein-protein interaction mechanism supported by citation.

claim: Upon Wnt activation, the destruction complex disassembles and β-catenin is no longer degraded.
source: As a consequence, the destruction complex disassembles, β-catenin is no longer degraded and translocates into the nucleus.
evidence: This describes the consequence of Wnt pathway activation based on established knowledge.

claim: β-catenin translocates into the nucleus upon Wnt activation.
source: As a consequence, the destruction complex disassembles, β-catenin is no longer degraded and translocates into the nucleus.
evidence: This describes nuclear translocation as part of Wnt signaling.

claim: In the nucleus, β-catenin interacts with the TCF/LEF family of transcription factors and activates target genes in a cell-type-dependent manner.
source: In the nucleus, β-catenin interacts with the T cell factor (TCF)/lymphoid enhancer-binding factor (LEF) family of transcription factors and activates target genes in a cell-type-dependent manner.
evidence: This describes the transcriptional function of β-catenin based on established knowledge.

claim: β-catenin is found at cell-cell adherens junctions mediating interactions between the cytoplasmic domain of cadherins and the actin cytoskeleton.
source: In addition to its role in Wnt signaling, β-catenin is also found at cell-cell adherens junctions (AJs) mediating the interactions between the cytoplasmic domain of cadherins and the actin cytoskeleton (Aberle et al., 1994; Hoschuetzky et al., 1994; Huber and Weis, 2001).
evidence: This describes the adhesion function of β-catenin supported by citations.

claim: The human β-catenin protein consists of 781 amino acids and contains three distinct structural domains.
source: The human β-catenin protein consists of 781 amino acids and contains three distinct structural domains.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the protein structure.

claim: Both N- and C-terminal domains of β-catenin are structurally flexible, whereas the central armadillo repeat has a rather rigid scaffold structure.
source: Crystal structure and NMR analysis of β-catenin have revealed that both N- and C-terminal domains are structurally flexible, whereas the central armadillo repeat has a rather rigid scaffold structure (Huber et al., 1997; Orsulic and Peifer, 1996; Xing et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes structural properties determined by experimental methods and supported by citations.

claim: The N-terminus of β-catenin is crucial for its stability and for cell adhesion by interacting with α-catenin.
source: The N-terminus is crucial for its stability and for cell adhesion by interacting with α-catenin.
evidence: This describes functional importance of a protein domain based on established knowledge.

claim: The N-terminal region of β-catenin contains evolutionarily conserved serine and tyrosine residues.
source: This region also contains evolutionarily conserved serine and tyrosine residues (Valenta et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes conserved residues supported by citation.

claim: Dysregulation of Wnt signaling components is associated with a variety of human diseases, ranging from growth-related pathologies to cancer.
source: Dysregulation of Wnt signaling components is associated with a variety of human diseases, ranging from growth-related pathologies to cancer (Clevers and Nusse, 2012; Zhan et al., 2017); however, overactive Wnt signaling has been difficult to target pharmacologically (Zhong and Virshup, 2020).
evidence: This statement about disease association is supported by citations.

claim: Overactive Wnt signaling has been difficult to target pharmacologically.
source: Dysregulation of Wnt signaling components is associated with a variety of human diseases, ranging from growth-related pathologies to cancer (Clevers and Nusse, 2012; Zhan et al., 2017); however, overactive Wnt signaling has been difficult to target pharmacologically (Zhong and Virshup, 2020).
evidence: This statement about therapeutic challenges is supported by citation.

claim: Mutations in CTNNB1/β-catenin in colorectal cancer are typically found in its N-terminal domain, particularly in exon 3.
source: Mutations in CTNNB1/β-catenin in colorectal cancer are typically found in its N-terminal domain, particularly in exon 3 that carries multiple phosphorylation sites for CK1 and GSK3β, including amino acids Ser33, Ser37, Thr41, and Ser45 (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Dar et al., 2017; Jamieson et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes mutation patterns in cancer supported by citations.

claim: Exon 3 of β-catenin carries multiple phosphorylation sites for CK1 and GSK3β, including amino acids Ser33, Ser37, Thr41, and Ser45.
source: Mutations in CTNNB1/β-catenin in colorectal cancer are typically found in its N-terminal domain, particularly in exon 3 that carries multiple phosphorylation sites for CK1 and GSK3β, including amino acids Ser33, Ser37, Thr41, and Ser45 (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Dar et al., 2017; Jamieson et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes specific phosphorylation sites supported by citations.

claim: Mutations or deletions of phosphorylation sites in β-catenin prevent phosphorylation, leading to its accumulation and subsequent activation of Wnt pathway target genes.
source: Mutations or deletions of these sites, often in only one allele, prevent phosphorylation of β-catenin, leading to its accumulation and subsequent activation of Wnt pathway target genes.
evidence: This describes the functional consequence of mutations based on established knowledge.

claim: Mutations or deletions of phosphorylation sites in β-catenin often occur in only one allele.
source: Mutations or deletions of these sites, often in only one allele, prevent phosphorylation of β-catenin, leading to its accumulation and subsequent activation of Wnt pathway target genes.
evidence: This describes the genetic pattern of mutations based on established knowledge.

claim: The biochemical and biophysical properties of different β-catenin alleles in their endogenous loci have remained largely unknown.
source: However, the biochemical and biophysical properties of different β-catenin alleles in their endogenous loci have remained largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Previous studies used overexpression of fluorescently tagged β-catenin to analyze its kinetics.
source: Previously, the dynamics and biochemical properties of β-catenin in cells were investigated by using transiently or stably overexpressed fluorescent fusion proteins (Giannini et al., 2000; Jamieson et al., 2011; Kafri et al., 2016; Krieghoff et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes previous experimental approaches supported by citations.

claim: HCT116 is a diploid colon cancer cell line that harbors both a wild-type and a ∆Ser45 mutant β-catenin allele.
source: To study wild-type and mutant β-catenin at physiological expression levels, we utilized the diploid colon cancer cell line HCT116 that harbors both a wild-type and a ∆Ser45 mutant allele.
evidence: This describes the genetic characteristics of the cell line used in the study.

claim: The in-frame ∆Ser45 deletion in β-catenin results in a loss of phosphorylation at this position, leading to the stabilization of β-catenin and constant activation of Wnt downstream targets.
source: This in-frame ∆Ser45 deletion results in a loss of phosphorylation at this position, leading to the stabilization of β-catenin and constant activation of Wnt downstream targets (Hagen and Vidal-Puig, 2002).
evidence: This describes the functional consequence of the mutation supported by citation.

claim: A gene replacement strategy using CRISPR/Cas9 editing was applied to introduce different fluorescent tags in the two alleles of the β-catenin locus of HCT116 cells in one step.
source: To generate endogenously tagged β-catenin, we applied a gene replacement strategy using CRISPR/Cas9 editing (Mali et al., 2013; Ran et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2014) to introduce different fluorescent tags in the two alleles of the β-catenin locus of HCT116 cells in one step (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach with citation support and reference to figures.

claim: C-terminal tagging of β-catenin did not affect β-catenin function in overexpression experiments.
source: This target site was chosen because it has previously been shown that C-terminal tagging did not affect β-catenin function in overexpression experiments (Giannini et al., 2000; Jamieson et al., 2011; Kafri et al., 2016; Krieghoff et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: mClover3 and mCherry2 were chosen for their favorable biophysical properties such as spectral absorbance, brightness, photostability, and maturation time.
source: We chose mClover3 and mCherry2 for their favorable biophysical properties such as spectral absorbance, brightness, photostability, and maturation time (Bajar et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2017; Thorn, 2017).
evidence: This describes the rationale for fluorophore selection supported by citations.

claim: FLAG and V5-tags were integrated between the C-terminal domain of β-catenin and the flexible GS linker to enable biochemical experiments.
source: Moreover, FLAG and V5-tags were integrated between the C-terminal domain of β-catenin and the flexible GS linker to enable biochemical experiments.
evidence: This describes the design of the tagging construct.

claim: A flexible GS linker consisting of three repeats of glycine and serine residues, (Gly-Gly-Gly-Gly-Ser)3, was inserted between the FLAG/V5 tags and the fluorescent proteins to avoid steric hindrance.
source: To avoid steric hindrance of the different domains, a flexible GS linker consisting of three repeats of glycine and serine residues, (Gly-Gly-Gly-Gly-Ser)3, was inserted between the FLAG/V5 tags and the fluorescent proteins (Trinh et al., 2004; Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the construct design with citation support and figure reference.

claim: Gene resistance cassettes flanked by loxP sites were introduced after the fluorescent proteins for selection of edited cells after homology-directed repair.
source: Gene resistance cassettes flanked by loxP sites were also introduced after the fluorescent proteins for selection of edited cells after homology-directed repair (HDR) (Smirnikhina et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the selection strategy with citation support.

claim: Selection cassettes encoded for antibiotic resistance to hygromycin and blasticidin on the Clover and Cherry donor templates, respectively.
source: Selection cassettes encoded for antibiotic resistance to hygromycin and blasticidin on the Clover and Cherry donor templates, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the selection markers used in the constructs.

claim: The loxP sites were included to allow resistance cassette removal upon expression of Cre recombinase.
source: The loxP sites were included to allow resistance cassette removal upon expression of Cre recombinase.
evidence: This describes the design feature for cassette removal.

claim: Infrequent fluorophore expression was observed, regardless of whether a single donor template was used or both donors were co-transfected simultaneously.
source: Infrequent fluorophore expression was observed, regardless of whether a single donor template was used (1.4% of Cherry- and 17.3% of Clover-labeled cells) or both donors were co-transfected simultaneously (0.9% of only Cherry-, 7.4% of only Clover-, and 0.1% of double-labeled cells) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes experimental results with specific percentages and figure reference.

claim: The donor template Clover was more efficiently integrated than the Cherry one.
source: The editing efficiency between the two donor templates was different. The donor template Clover was more efficiently integrated than the Cherry one.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: In total, 44 single-cell clones were sorted by FACS and expanded for further characterization.
source: In total, 44 single-cell clones were sorted by FACS and expanded for further characterization, which included double-positive and single-positive cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and sample size.

claim: Only one single clone (#37) appeared to have the correct insertion of both fluorophores in the β-catenin/CTNNB1 locus.
source: All 44 clones were analyzed by allele-specific PCR and most of them were sequenced from the 5′ junction of the integration cassette. Only one single clone (#37) appeared to have the correct insertion of both fluorophores in the β-catenin/CTNNB1 locus.
evidence: This describes the outcome of genotyping analysis.

claim: 7 clones showed a heterozygous integration of the Cherry fluorophore in the β-catenin/CTNNB1 locus.
source: In addition, 7 clones showed a heterozygous integration of the Cherry fluorophore in the β-catenin/CTNNB1 locus, and 24 clones were heterozygous for the Clover fluorophore-tagged allele.
evidence: This describes the genotyping results for specific clones.

claim: 24 clones were heterozygous for the Clover fluorophore-tagged allele.
source: In addition, 7 clones showed a heterozygous integration of the Cherry fluorophore in the β-catenin/CTNNB1 locus, and 24 clones were heterozygous for the Clover fluorophore-tagged allele.
evidence: This describes the genotyping results for specific clones.

claim: Six clones had an insertion of the donor cassette after the stop codon of β-catenin/CTNNB1.
source: Moreover, six clones had an insertion of the donor cassette after the stop codon of β-catenin/CTNNB1.
evidence: This describes incorrect integration events.

claim: Two isogenic cell lines had partial integration of the Clover tag.
source: Two isogenic cell lines had partial integration of the Clover tag and four clones were wild-type indicating no editing events in the CTNNB1 locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes the genotyping results.

claim: Four clones were wild-type indicating no editing events in the CTNNB1 locus.
source: Two isogenic cell lines had partial integration of the Clover tag and four clones were wild-type indicating no editing events in the CTNNB1 locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes the genotyping results.

claim: Clone #37 had one allele tagged with Cherry and the other one tagged with Clover.
source: Taken together, these experiments indicate that single-cell clones #24 and #33 had the Clover donor construct inserted in one CTNNB1 allele, clone #45 had the Cherry tag inserted in one allele, and clone #37 had one allele tagged with Cherry and the other one tagged with Clover.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple genotyping experiments.

claim: Sequencing revealed correct in-frame integration of the fluorophore sequences at the 3′ end of the CTNNB1/β-catenin coding sequence.
source: Next, we sequenced the amplicons from our genotyping PCRs (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4). This revealed correct in-frame integration of the fluorophore sequences at the 3′ end of the CTNNB1/β-catenin coding sequence.
evidence: This describes sequencing results confirming correct integration.

claim: The untagged allele was not altered at the sgRNA target site in clones #24 and #45.
source: We also confirmed that one CTNNB1 allele remained untagged in clones #24, #33, and #45. While the untagged allele was not altered at the sgRNA target site in clones #24 and #45, we detected a 40-bp mutation in clone #33, presumably from error-prone non-homologous end joining of a Cas9-induced double-strand break.
evidence: This describes sequencing results for the untagged allele.

claim: A 40-bp mutation was detected in clone #33, presumably from error-prone non-homologous end joining of a Cas9-induced double-strand break.
source: While the untagged allele was not altered at the sgRNA target site in clones #24 and #45, we detected a 40-bp mutation in clone #33, presumably from error-prone non-homologous end joining of a Cas9-induced double-strand break.
evidence: This describes a mutation with inference about its origin.

claim: The 40-bp mutation in clone #33 results in four additional amino acids at the end of β-catenin.
source: This mutation results in four additional amino acids at the end of β-catenin.
evidence: This describes the consequence of the mutation.

claim: Sequencing of the bi-allelically tagged clone #37 revealed that both alleles had been modified without unintended mutations.
source: Importantly, sequencing of the bi-allelically tagged clone #37 revealed that both alleles had been modified without unintended mutations (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This describes sequencing results confirming correct editing.

claim: Both clones #37 and #45 carried the Cherry fluorophore in the ∆Ser45 allele.
source: Sanger sequencing of cDNA templates revealed that both clones #37 and #45 carried the Cherry fluorophore in the ∆Ser45 allele (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes sequencing results identifying which allele was tagged.

claim: Clones #33 and #37 harbored the Clover fluorophore in the wild-type allele.
source: In contrast, clones #33 and #37 harbored the Clover fluorophore in the wild-type allele, as indicated by the in-frame sequence with Ser45.
evidence: This describes sequencing results identifying which allele was tagged.

claim: Clone #37 has two high molecular weight bands indicative of both tagged β-catenin variants.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, clones #33 and #45 have one of the tagged variants of β-catenin, whereas clone #37 has two high molecular weight bands indicative of both tagged β-catenin variants.
evidence: This describes Western blot results.

claim: GFP-immunoprecipitated lysates of clone #37 showed a β-catenin variant with molecular mass higher than 97 kDa that was recognized by β-catenin, GFP, and Flag antibodies.
source: GFP-immunoprecipitated lysates of clone #37 (Figure 2C), a β-catenin variant with molecular mass higher than 97 kDa was recognized by β-catenin, GFP, and Flag antibodies.
evidence: This describes immunoprecipitation results.

claim: Upon RFP/Cherry immunoprecipitation of clone #37, a band around 97 kDa was detected by β-catenin, Cherry and V5 antibodies.
source: By contrast, upon RFP/Cherry immunoprecipitation a band around 97 kDa was detected by β-catenin, Cherry and V5 antibodies.
evidence: This describes immunoprecipitation results.

claim: Pulldown with a β-catenin antibody demonstrated two different β-catenin variants that were either detected by GFP/Flag or Cherry/V5 antibodies.
source: Pulldown with a β-catenin antibody demonstrated two different β-catenin variants that were either detected by GFP/Flag or Cherry/V5 antibodies.
evidence: This describes immunoprecipitation results confirming two distinct tagged variants.

claim: Wild-type β-catenin-Clover protein runs higher than 97 kDa and is recognized by both GFP and Flag antibodies.
source: Wild-type β-catenin-Clover protein runs higher than 97 kDa and it is recognized by both GFP and Flag antibodies (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the molecular weight and antibody recognition of the tagged protein.

claim: Mutant β-catenin-Cherry protein runs around 97 kDa as a single band in whole-cell lysate.
source: Mutant β-catenin-Cherry protein runs around 97 kDa as a single band, as detected in the whole-cell lysate (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This describes the molecular weight of the tagged protein.

claim: Upon immunoprecipitation with RFP beads, several bands of mutant β-catenin-Cherry are frequently detected.
source: Upon immunoprecipitation, especially with RFP beads, several bands of mutant β-catenin-Cherry are frequently detected.
evidence: This describes an observation from immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: All three antibodies (β-catenin, GFP, and Flag) detected only one band representing the mutant β-catenin-Clover protein in clone #24.
source: To evaluate whether this is due to modifications of mutant β-catenin or due to the Cherry-tag itself, we analyzed clone #24 expressing a mutant β-catenin tagged with Clover. All three antibodies, β-catenin, GFP, and Flag, detected only one band representing the mutant β-catenin-Clover protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the additional bands of mutant β-catenin-Cherry arise from the Cherry-tag.
evidence: This describes experimental results that support an inference about the origin of multiple bands.

claim: The additional bands of mutant β-catenin-Cherry arise from the Cherry-tag.
source: All three antibodies, β-catenin, GFP, and Flag, detected only one band representing the mutant β-catenin-Clover protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the additional bands of mutant β-catenin-Cherry arise from the Cherry-tag.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing different tagged versions.

claim: The mCherry protein may undergo chemical modification during sample preparation by TCEP in the loading dye.
source: One possible explanation is that the mCherry protein undergoes chemical modification during sample preparation, for example, by TCEP in the loading dye (Cloin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation.

claim: mCherry might undergo backbone cleavage during chromophore maturation.
source: Alternatively, mCherry might undergo backbone cleavage during chromophore maturation (Barondeau et al., 2006; Nienhaus et al., 2005; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: Backbone cleavage during maturation does not impair the fluorescence emission of mCherry, as fragments remain tightly associated to form the fluorescent beta-barrel structure.
source: Importantly, such cleavage during maturation does not impair the fluorescence emission, as fragments remain tightly associated to form the fluorescent beta-barrel structure (Barondeau et al., 2006; Nienhaus et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: All three clones #33, #37, and #45 showed a similar growth behavior as the parental β-cateninWT/∆45 cells.
source: All three clones #33, #37, and #45 showed a similar growth behavior as the parental β-cateninWT/∆45 cells (Figure 3A), whereas the cell line carrying a single wild-type allele (β-cateninWT+/−) displayed impaired growth.
evidence: This describes proliferation assay results.

claim: The cell line carrying a single wild-type allele (β-cateninWT+/−) displayed impaired growth.
source: All three clones #33, #37, and #45 showed a similar growth behavior as the parental β-cateninWT/∆45 cells (Figure 3A), whereas the cell line carrying a single wild-type allele (β-cateninWT+/−) displayed impaired growth.
evidence: This describes proliferation assay results.

claim: Downregulation of β-catenin led to the reduction in fluorophore levels as well as the Wnt target gene AXIN2.
source: We found that downregulation of β-catenin led to the reduction in fluorophore levels as well as the Wnt target gene AXIN2.
evidence: This describes RT-qPCR results from siRNA experiments.

claim: Depletion of β-catenin resulted in a reduction of Cherry and Clover on the protein level.
source: Consistently, depletion of β-catenin resulted in a reduction of Cherry and Clover, as shown by immunofluorescence on the protein level (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes immunofluorescence results from siRNA experiments.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis confirmed the localization of the endogenously tagged β-catenin variants at the cell membrane as observed in the parental HCT116 cell line.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis confirmed the localization of the endogenously tagged β-catenin variants at the cell membrane as observed in the parental HCT116 cell line (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes immunofluorescence results showing subcellular localization.

claim: Immunoprecipitation with an E-cadherin antibody demonstrated the interaction of β-catenin and E-cadherin in all clones.
source: Immunoprecipitation with an E-cadherin antibody demonstrated the interaction of β-catenin and E-cadherin in all clones (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes immunoprecipitation results showing protein-protein interaction.

claim: Endogenously tagging of β-catenin did not affect its localization and adhesive function.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that endogenously tagging of β-catenin did neither affect its localization and adhesive function nor its ability to activate the Wnt pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple functional assays.

claim: Endogenously tagging of β-catenin did not affect its ability to activate the Wnt pathway.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that endogenously tagging of β-catenin did neither affect its localization and adhesive function nor its ability to activate the Wnt pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple functional assays.

claim: Upon CHIR99021 treatment, TCF4/Wnt-reporter activity was induced and AXIN2 gene expression levels were increased similarly in all isogenic cell lines.
source: Upon CHIR99021 treatment, TCF4/Wnt-reporter activity was induced and AXIN2 gene expression levels were increased similarly in all isogenic cell lines.
evidence: This describes results from reporter assays and RT-qPCR.

claim: Treatment with the Wnt inhibitor ICG001 decreased Wnt reporter activity and AXIN2 expression levels in all cell lines.
source: Treatment with the Wnt inhibitor ICG001 decreased Wnt reporter activity and AXIN2 expression levels in all cell lines, as expected (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes results from reporter assays and RT-qPCR.

claim: After addition of CHIR99021, nuclear β-catenin was increased in all clones indicative of increased nuclear translocation of β-catenin upon Wnt activation.
source: In addition, immunofluorescence analysis demonstrated that after addition of CHIR99021, nuclear β-catenin was increased in all clones indicative of increased nuclear translocation of β-catenin upon Wnt activation (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This describes immunofluorescence results with inference about mechanism.

claim: Treatment with ICG001 did not affect cytoplasmic or nuclear β-catenin localization in the endogenously tagged or parental cell clones.
source: Consistent with its mechanism of action, treatment with ICG001 did neither affect cytoplasmic nor nuclear β-catenin localization in the endogenously tagged or parental cell clones.
evidence: This describes immunofluorescence results.

claim: Upon inhibition of Wnt secretion by addition of porcupine inhibitor LGK974, the signal of both mutant and wild-type β-catenin allele decreased but could be rescued by addition of recombinant Wnt3a.
source: Upon inhibition of Wnt secretion by addition of porcupine inhibitor LGK974, the signal of both, mutant as well as wild-type β-catenin allele, decreased but could be rescued by addition of recombinant Wnt3a (Figure 4C).
evidence: This describes experimental results from drug treatment and rescue experiments.

claim: Silencing of either Clover or Cherry in clone #37 reduced β-catenin and AXIN2 expression levels in a similar manner.
source: Silencing of either Clover or Cherry in clone #37 reduced β-catenin and AXIN2 expression levels in a similar manner, whereas combined knockdown of both had an additive effect comparable to siRNA β-catenin/CTNNB1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes RT-qPCR results from allele-specific knockdown experiments.

claim: Combined knockdown of both Clover and Cherry had an additive effect comparable to siRNA β-catenin/CTNNB1.
source: Silencing of either Clover or Cherry in clone #37 reduced β-catenin and AXIN2 expression levels in a similar manner, whereas combined knockdown of both had an additive effect comparable to siRNA β-catenin/CTNNB1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes RT-qPCR results from allele-specific knockdown experiments.

claim: Both wild-type and mutant β-catenin alleles contribute to Wnt activity.
source: These results indicate that both wild-type and mutant β-catenin alleles contribute to Wnt activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from allele-specific knockdown experiments.

claim: Wnt secretion is essential for maintaining Wnt activity in HCT116 cells.
source: This is also consistent with previous results in HCT116 cells demonstrating that Wnt secretion is essential for maintaining Wnt activity (Voloshanenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The median diffusion coefficient of mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin in the cytosol is 10.6 ± 1.8 µm² s–1.
source: On the basis of FCS experiments in the cytosol of more than 40 cells, we calculated a median D value of 10.6 ± 1.8 µm² s–1 for mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin, which is significantly smaller than the one of wild-type Clover-tagged β-catenin (D=17.3 ± 6.1 µm² s–1, Figure 6A).
evidence: This describes quantitative FCS measurements.

claim: The median diffusion coefficient of wild-type Clover-tagged β-catenin in the cytosol is 17.3 ± 6.1 µm² s–1.
source: On the basis of FCS experiments in the cytosol of more than 40 cells, we calculated a median D value of 10.6 ± 1.8 µm² s–1 for mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin, which is significantly smaller than the one of wild-type Clover-tagged β-catenin (D=17.3 ± 6.1 µm² s–1, Figure 6A).
evidence: This describes quantitative FCS measurements.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin is significantly smaller than that of wild-type Clover-tagged β-catenin.
source: On the basis of FCS experiments in the cytosol of more than 40 cells, we calculated a median D value of 10.6 ± 1.8 µm² s–1 for mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin, which is significantly smaller than the one of wild-type Clover-tagged β-catenin (D=17.3 ± 6.1 µm² s–1, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of FCS measurements.

claim: The ratio of diffusion coefficients indicates that mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin diffuses as part of a larger complex, with a more than fourfold larger volume/overall mass than wild-type Clover-tagged β-catenin.
source: The ratio of diffusion coefficients indicates that mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin diffuses as part of a larger complex, with a more than fourfold larger volume/overall mass than wild-type Clover-tagged β-catenin.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the diffusion coefficient measurements based on the Stokes-Einstein relationship.

claim: The concentration of wild-type Clover-tagged β-catenin in the cytosol is 32 ± 9 nM.
source: From the autocorrelation amplitudes in the green and red color channels, the concentrations of wild-type Clover-tagged β-catenin and mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin were determined as 32 ± 9 nM and 75 ± 11 nM (medians of distributions over more than 40 cells, Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This describes quantitative FCS measurements of protein concentration.

claim: The concentration of mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin in the cytosol is 75 ± 11 nM.
source: From the autocorrelation amplitudes in the green and red color channels, the concentrations of wild-type Clover-tagged β-catenin and mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin were determined as 32 ± 9 nM and 75 ± 11 nM (medians of distributions over more than 40 cells, Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This describes quantitative FCS measurements of protein concentration.

claim: The measured β-catenin concentrations agree well with previous measurements in the RKO cell line, which revealed β-catenin concentrations of ~52 nM upon Wnt3A stimulation.
source: These data agree well with previous measurements in the RKO cell line, which revealed β-catenin concentrations of ~52 nM upon Wnt3A stimulation (Hernández et al., 2012) and in HEK293T and colon cancer cell lines (Tan et al., 2012).
evidence: This compares current measurements to previous studies with citation support.

claim: Treatment with CHIR99021 changed the diffusion coefficients and concentrations of wild-type β-catenin so that they became similar to those of mutant β-catenin.
source: Interestingly, treatment with CHIR99021 changed the diffusion coefficients and concentrations of wild-type β-catenin so that they became similar to the ones of mutant β-catenin, whereas smaller effects were observed for the mutant isoform.
evidence: This describes FCS results from drug treatment experiments.

claim: Treatment with CHIR99021 had smaller effects on the mutant β-catenin isoform compared to wild-type.
source: Interestingly, treatment with CHIR99021 changed the diffusion coefficients and concentrations of wild-type β-catenin so that they became similar to the ones of mutant β-catenin, whereas smaller effects were observed for the mutant isoform.
evidence: This describes FCS results from drug treatment experiments.

claim: GSK3β inhibition renders the concentration and diffusional dynamics of wild-type β-catenin such that they are in the range of those of the mutant isoform.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that GSK3β inhibition renders the concentration and diffusional dynamics of wild-type β-catenin such that they are in the range of those of the mutant isoform.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from FCS measurements under different conditions.

claim: Upon LGK974 treatment, the concentration of wild-type β-catenin was reduced.
source: Upon this treatment, the concentration of wild-type β-catenin was found to be reduced, whereas the decrease of mutant β-catenin concentration was less pronounced.
evidence: This describes FCS results from inhibitor treatment.

claim: Upon LGK974 treatment, the decrease of mutant β-catenin concentration was less pronounced compared to wild-type.
source: Upon this treatment, the concentration of wild-type β-catenin was found to be reduced, whereas the decrease of mutant β-catenin concentration was less pronounced.
evidence: This describes FCS results from inhibitor treatment.

claim: The concentration changes caused by LGK974 could be rescued by addition of recombinant Wnt3a.
source: These concentration changes could be rescued by addition of recombinant Wnt3a, whereas addition of recombinant Wnt3a to cells without inhibitor treatment increased the wild-type β-catenin amount only slightly (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes FCS results from rescue experiments.

claim: Upon LGK974 treatment, the diffusivity of the Clover-tagged β-catenin fraction was two times as large as for the control.
source: Upon LGK974 treatment, the diffusivity of the Clover-tagged β-catenin fraction was two times as large as for the control, DWT,LGK=24.0 ± 2.8 µm² s−1; however, the diffusivity of the mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin fraction did not increase (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes quantitative FCS measurements under inhibitor treatment.

claim: The diffusivity of the mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin fraction did not increase upon LGK974 treatment.
source: Upon LGK974 treatment, the diffusivity of the Clover-tagged β-catenin fraction was two times as large as for the control, DWT,LGK=24.0 ± 2.8 µm² s−1; however, the diffusivity of the mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin fraction did not increase (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes quantitative FCS measurements under inhibitor treatment.

claim: Additional Wnt3a treatment reversed the effect of LGK974 treatment on the diffusivity of wild-type β-catenin.
source: Additional Wnt3a treatment reversed the effect of LGK974 treatment on the diffusivity of wild-type β-catenin. The FCS analysis yielded DWT,LGK+Wnt3a=11.6 ± 2.3 µm² s−1, which is essentially identical to that of the control.
evidence: This describes FCS results from rescue experiments.

claim: APC mutations are frequently found in colorectal cancer and define the onset of the transition from adenoma to carcinoma.
source: APC mutations are frequently found in colorectal cancer and define the onset of the transition from adenoma to carcinoma.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer genetics.

claim: The complete loss of APC is very rare; truncating mutations lacking the C-terminal domain are frequently observed.
source: The complete loss of APC is very rare; truncating mutations lacking the C-terminal domain are, however, frequently observed (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Fearnhead et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement about mutation patterns is supported by citations.

claim: In the cytosol and nucleus of APCLOF cells, the concentration and diffusional dynamics of wild-type β-catenin were different in comparison to cells with wild-type APC.
source: In the cytosol (Figure 7B) and in the nucleus (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) of APCLOF cells, the concentration and diffusional dynamics of wild-type β-catenin were different in comparison to cells with wild-type APC.
evidence: This describes FCS results comparing cells with different APC genotypes.

claim: Both wild-type β-catenin-Clover and mutant β-catenin-Cherry bind to APC, Axin1, and GSK3β.
source: Both wild-type β-catenin-Clover and mutant β-catenin-Cherry bind to APC, Axin1, and GSK3β (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), indicating that both isoforms are part of the destruction complex.
evidence: This describes immunoprecipitation results with inference about complex membership.

claim: Both wild-type and mutant β-catenin isoforms are part of the destruction complex.
source: Both wild-type β-catenin-Clover and mutant β-catenin-Cherry bind to APC, Axin1, and GSK3β (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), indicating that both isoforms are part of the destruction complex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from immunoprecipitation results.

claim: Both alleles of β-catenin can be regulated by the destruction complex but the level of regulation is different.
source: Both alleles of β-catenin can be regulated by the destruction complex but the level of regulation is different.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Mutant β-catenin shows slight regulation upon inhibition of GSK3β or truncation of APC while the wild-type allele is more sensitive to these perturbations.
source: Mutant β-catenin shows slight regulation upon inhibition of GSK3β or truncation of APC while the wild-type allele is more sensitive to these perturbations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from FCS measurements under different conditions.

claim: Mutations in β-catenin that activate the Wnt pathway occur in about 5% of colorectal and more than 25% of liver and uterine tumors.
source: Mutations in β-catenin that activate the Wnt pathway occur in about 5% of colorectal and more than 25% of liver and uterine tumors (Hoadley et al., 2018; Sanchez-Vega et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement about mutation frequencies is supported by citations.

claim: The investigation of β-catenin's biochemical properties has been hampered by the lack of suitable tools to study its function at a physiological level.
source: Nevertheless, the investigation of its biochemical properties has been hampered by the lack of suitable tools to study its function at a physiological level.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations in the field.

claim: Advances in genome editing methods such as CRISPR/Cas9 enable the modification of endogenous loci and the manipulations of genes for applications such as endogenous tagging of genes.
source: Advances in genome editing methods such as CRISPR/Cas9 enable the modification of endogenous loci and the manipulations of genes for applications such as endogenous tagging of genes (Cong et al., 2013; Dambournet et al., 2014; Mali et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement about technological capabilities is supported by citations.

claim: The efficiency of HDR depends not only on homology arms but also on the integrated sequence.
source: Surprisingly, the efficiency of integration of the two donor templates was different, with Clover having about a 12-fold better integration efficiency than Cherry (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B). This might indicate that the efficiency of HDR depends not only on homology arms but also on the integrated sequence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observed differences in integration efficiency.

claim: Previous overexpression studies showed that C-terminal tagging of β-catenin did not affect its functions.
source: While tagging of proteins can interfere with protein functions, it can also lead to the accumulation of the protein and its potential overactivation. In line with our study, previous overexpression studies showed that C-terminal tagging of β-catenin did not affect its functions (Giannini et al., 2000; Jamieson et al., 2011; Kafri et al., 2016; Krieghoff et al., 2006; Orsulic and Peifer, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inactivation of β-catenin or canonical Wnt signaling in HCT116 cells has been previously shown to inhibit proliferation.
source: In contrast, inactivation of β-catenin or canonical Wnt signaling in HCT116 cells has been previously shown to inhibit proliferation (Scholer-Dahirel et al., 2011; Voloshanenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The region required for β-catenin's adhesion function is within the central part of β-catenin and not at the C-terminus.
source: The region required for its adhesion function is within the central part of β-catenin and not at the C-terminus (Valenta et al., 2012; Xing et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: A similar diffusion coefficient was recently determined by FCS for β-catenin endogenously tagged with monomeric SGFP2 in HAP1 cells.
source: In support of our data, a similar diffusion coefficient was recently determined by FCS for β-catenin endogenously tagged with monomeric SGFP2 in HAP1 cells (de Man et al., 2021).
evidence: This compares current results to a recent study with citation support.

claim: Previous reports indicated that β-catenin mutants with deletion or mutation of Ser 45 retain signaling activity and are still responsive toward Wnt activation.
source: Previous reports indicated that β-catenin mutants with deletion or mutation of Ser 45 retain signaling activity and are still responsive toward Wnt activation (Chan et al., 2002; Parker et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FRAP analysis demonstrated that TCF4, APC, Axin, and Axin2 reduced β-catenin mobility and nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling.
source: Along this line, FRAP analysis demonstrated that TCF4, APC, Axin, and Axin2 reduced β-catenin mobility and nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling suggesting that these interaction partners control the subcellular localization of β-catenin by sequestering it in the respective compartment (Krieghoff et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Structural changes of β-catenin rather than molecule numbers regulate Wnt signaling.
source: Accordingly, Goentoro and Kirschner, 2009 demonstrated that structural changes of β-catenin rather than molecule numbers regulate Wnt signaling (Goentoro and Kirschner, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation.

claim: A recent FCS-based study in HAP1 cells showed that Wnt pathway activation regulates the distribution of free β-catenin and β-catenin bound in multi-protein complexes between nucleus and cytosol.
source: Furthermore, a recent FCS-based study in HAP1 cells showed that Wnt pathway activation regulates the distribution of free β-catenin and β-catenin bound in multi-protein complexes between nucleus and cytosol by modulating β-catenin destruction, shuttling between cytoplasm and nucleus, and nuclear retention (de Man et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Most cytosolic β-catenin exists in a monomeric form, whereas dimers of α-catenin and β-catenin interacted mainly with cadherin.
source: Moreover, different molecular forms of β-catenin have been described, demonstrating that most cytosolic β-catenin exists in a monomeric form, whereas dimers of α-catenin and β-catenin interacted mainly with cadherin (Gottardi and Gumbiner, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation.

claim: Immunoprecipitation and FCS analyses indicate that wild-type and mutant β-catenin are found in two separate pools.
source: Interestingly, our immunoprecipitation and FCS analyses indicate that wild-type and mutant β-catenin are found in two separate pools.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental approaches.

claim: β-catenin is mobile in both cytoplasmic and nuclear compartments, with mutant β-catenin being found in higher molecular weight complexes.
source: We observed that β-catenin is mobile in both compartments, with mutant β-catenin being found in higher molecular weight complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from FCS measurements.

claim: Cross-correlation amplitudes between wild-type Clover-tagged and mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin were always found to be zero within the experimental error.
source: Cross-correlation amplitudes between wild-type Clover-tagged and mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin were always found to be zero within the experimental error, implying that these two β-catenin variants diffuse independently and do not associate to any significant degree (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes FCS cross-correlation analysis results with inference about protein interactions.

claim: Wild-type Clover-tagged and mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin diffuse independently and do not associate to any significant degree.
source: Cross-correlation amplitudes between wild-type Clover-tagged and mutant Cherry-tagged β-catenin were always found to be zero within the experimental error, implying that these two β-catenin variants diffuse independently and do not associate to any significant degree (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cross-correlation analysis.
